beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. An agent's description isn't a résumé — it's the trigger clause Claude scans before dispatch. List capabilities and nothing fires. State when to reach for it and it fires. So: does listing my agent's triggers tell Claude when to use it?

beats.narration_text: Take the file apart. Two parts: YAML frontmatter — the machine-readable header Claude parses — then a markdown body it reads once dispatched. Five frontmatter fields. Name: lowercase, hyphens, three to fifty characters, alphanumeric on both ends — code-reviewer, test-generator, security-analyzer. Description: the field that carries the whole file, because it's loaded into Claude's context the moment the agent is registered, and it's what Claude reads to decide whether to dispatch this agent at all. Model: inherit is the recommended default — it keeps you on the main session's model. Color is cosmetic, a chip in the interface, nothing more. Tools: the array of permissions the agent gets; give it only what the task needs, because that array is the whole security surface. Underneath the frontmatter, the body: role, output format, and a When to invoke section with worked scenarios. They optimized for keeping dispatch-time context small — only the description travels to Claude at decision time; the body stays on disk until the agent is actually chosen.

Now the description's actual job. State exactly when Claude should reach for this agent — the trigger, not the résumé. The convention is a shape you follow: 'Use this agent when...' then 'Typical triggers include' two to four concrete scenarios, then a pointer to a When to invoke section down in the body. That prose has to name real triggers — proactive and reactive, different phrasings of the same underlying request — and it has to name when not to use the agent, because a false-positive dispatch costs a wasted call. Down in the body, the When to invoke section does the same work at higher resolution: a bold scenario name, what the situation looks like, what the agent does when it fires. Same triggers, two audiences. The description is written for Claude's dispatch decision at registration time. The body is written for the agent once it's already running.

Here's the cost of writing the same triggers twice. Nothing keeps the two copies in sync. Change a trigger and update only the description — the body's When to invoke section goes stale. Update only the body — the description falls behind. And because it's the description alone that Claude reads at dispatch time, any scenario that only lives in the stale body is invisible when the choice is being made. That trigger never even gets checked. They optimized for keeping dispatch-time context small: the body doesn't travel with the decision. The cost is a hand-maintained mirror — every time triggers change, you edit both files, in both places, correctly, or the agent starts misfiring in ways that don't leave a stack trace.
A subagent only fires when its description names the trigger conditions — not the capabilities. The best-written agent on your machine never gets dispatched if its description reads like a résumé.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm building a custom Claude Code subagent as part of a plugin, and I want the dispatch to actually fire when the situation matches. One — write the YAML frontmatter for an agent that reviews pull-request diffs for security issues: choose a name that meets the format rules, and write a description that opens with 'Use this agent when...' followed by 'Typical triggers include' two to four concrete scenarios, and ends with a pointer to a When to invoke section in the body. Two — write the body's When to invoke section: for each trigger, give it a bold scenario name, what the situation looks like on the pull request, and what the agent should do. Three — pick the minimum tools array, probably Read and Bash, and explain in one line why Write is not on that list. Four — critique your own description: which of your triggers is weakest, and rewrite it to be more concretely dispatchable. Go deeper: ask the same model what happens when your description's triggers and the body's When to invoke section drift out of sync — which one does Claude actually read at dispatch time, and design a small pre-commit check that fails when the two copies disagree.
